item: Rope with a ceiling suction cup
trueExplanation: Designed for window cleaners who enjoy extreme sports and zero safety guarantees.
heistExplanation: It looks like an action-movie prop, but in this case it genuinely helped someone get where gravity said no.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief reached an upper window from the outer wall, bypassing the castle's gates and guard post.
The rope let the thief cross a vertical interior space and reach a balcony above the protected display.
The suction rig provided an escape down the outer wall before the guards could secure the courtyard exits.

item: Lockpick set hidden inside a pen
trueExplanation: It actually writes quite nicely, assuming you don't accidentally press the secret pick-release button mid-signature.
heistExplanation: The pen is entirely innocent right up until it starts opening centuries-old mahogany doors.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The disguised picks opened a side door without forcing the lock or carrying an obvious burglary tool.
The pen opened the old display lock with enough precision to leave no sign that the case had been touched.
Because it looked like a pen, the tool passed through a casual security check without inviting questions.

trueExplanation: Printed on a home inkjet printer that was clearly running out of yellow ink.
heistExplanation: The best fake is the one everyone treats as completely normal because nobody gets paid enough to check holograms.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The fake pass got the thief through the conservation entrance as someone expected to handle delicate objects.
The pass gave the thief a mundane professional identity, making a long inspection of the display look routine.
The thief presented the pass as authorisation to remove the artifact for an invented conservation emergency.

item: Tablet with an open surveillance system
trueExplanation: The screen is covered in greasy fingerprints and currently streaming a live feed of the empty janitor's closet.
heistExplanation: Someone really did not want to guess where the security was looking, so they bought VIP front-row seats to the cameras.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief used the live feeds to identify the one camera rotation that left the display unobserved.
Watching the patrol cameras allowed the thief to move only when every guard was facing another direction.
The thief used the tablet's logged-in control session to suppress a camera alert before crossing the protected corridor and attack.

item: Mini camera hidden in a statue
trueExplanation: The camera lens occupies the statue's left nostril, giving every recording a uniquely unflattering angle.
heistExplanation: The statue looked patriotic and solemn, but inside it had the ambitions and eye line of a dedicated spy.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The hidden camera revealed exactly when the guards turned away from the display, creating a reliable window to act.
The thief reviewed the statue camera's recordings to learn the guard routes before moving through the castle.
The camera's view let an accomplice create a distraction at the exact moment the nearest guard was most vulnerable to it.

trueExplanation: Originally bought in a 10-pack for cleaning laptop screens and expensive sunglasses.
heistExplanation: Someone here really did not want to leave even a single fingerprint for eager forensic interns to find.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The gloves allowed the thief to handle the artifact and display hardware without leaving fingerprints behind.
The thief used the gloves to lift a key or access card from a guard without leaving an obvious trace.
The gloves wiped down touched surfaces as the thief moved, making the route look as though nobody had used it.

item: Shoe print on the polished floor
trueExplanation: A tragic reminder that the castle floor was waxed exactly four minutes before the break-in.
heistExplanation: This is not subtle decoration. Someone genuinely signed the crime scene floor with a muddy designer sneaker.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief followed the guard's fresh footprints to learn which corridor had just been cleared and moved through the opposite one.
The thief used the marks on the polished floor to identify the least-used route toward the courtyard exit.
A deliberately planted print sent guards tracking a fake intruder route while the thief used another exit.

item: Fragment of amber from a necklace
trueExplanation: It has a prehistoric mosquito inside that looks just as disappointed as the detective.
heistExplanation: Amber always looks noble and ancient, even when it is lying face-down under a dusty folding chair.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The amber fragment identified which necklace was the genuine historic piece rather than a display replica.
The thief used the fragment to confirm the necklace's material before removing the correct artifact from a crowded display.
The thief used a matching amber fragment to make a substituted necklace look intact from a casual distance.

trueExplanation: Page 42 is missing, replaced by a sticky note reading "Borrowed by Dave, back soon".
heistExplanation: The most suspicious thing in a museum is often the item that looks too properly documented to be part of a crime.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The inventory book identified the artifact with the highest value and the weakest recent audit history.
The thief altered the inventory trail so the missing object appeared to be on an authorised loan.
The records told the thief exactly which display held the original rather than a copy or a temporary substitute.

trueExplanation: Pointed at the courtyard, currently amplifying the sound of three pigeons fighting over a pretzel crust.
heistExplanation: This is not music equipment; it is a high-tech machine designed strictly for collecting other people's secrets.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief listened to courtyard patrols and moved only while the guards were committed to another route.
The microphone revealed which guard was most likely to respond to a false call, letting the thief pull them away at the right time.
Listening to control-room chatter told the thief when the camera operator was distracted, creating a brief unmonitored window.

trueExplanation: Contains three fake moustaches, two synthetic wigs, and a small tube of theatrical spirit gum.
heistExplanation: A cheap wig and round glasses can accomplish more than half the elaborate alibis in this building.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief used the kit to resemble a staff member expected in the conservation wing.
A changed face, hair, and posture made witnesses describe the costume rather than the thief.
The thief disguised an accomplice as a distressed visitor, drawing guards away from the exhibit.

trueExplanation: Includes very precise measurements of the main hall, alongside a surprisingly accurate recipe for garlic bread.
heistExplanation: Someone here clearly did their homework in both Renaissance architecture and high-stakes burglary.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The floor plan let the thief use service corridors and dead ends that never appear on visitor maps.
The layout revealed a corner where the two nearest cameras could not cover each other.
The thief marked a route from the display to a delivery exit before entering the castle.

trueExplanation: Drawn in 1742, meaning half the doors marked on it are now solid stone or gift shops.
heistExplanation: Old maps always promise secret passageways, and sometimes just deliver very bad, dead-end navigation.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The old map revealed a blocked-looking side entrance that still opened into a forgotten service passage.
The thief followed an old route through the castle that modern guards no longer considered part of their patrol area.
The map led to a little-used postern exit behind the old curtain wall.

trueExplanation: A warning sticker reads "DANGER 220V", which someone covered with a sticker of a cartoon cat.
heistExplanation: When an electrical junction box is left open with freshly cut wires, someone was planning more than a routine lightbulb change.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief cut power to one alarm zone while leaving the rest of the castle lit and apparently normal.
The junction box gave the thief physical access to the security wiring without needing the protected control panel.
The thief interrupted the power line feeding one camera, creating a dark patch beside the target room.

item: Climbing belt hooked to a balcony
trueExplanation: Officially left there by the window cleaning service, though nobody has seen them since Tuesday.
heistExplanation: Scaling a 15th-century castle facade in the dark requires either supreme confidence or extremely questionable life choices.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief climbed from the balcony to an upper window, bypassing every guarded entrance below.
The belt let the thief cross from the balcony to a high exterior ledge beside the secured room.
The balcony route provided a way down the outer facade while guards sealed the main castle exits.

trueExplanation: Composed using cutout magazine letters, mostly from a high-end gardening monthly.
heistExplanation: Some letters carry more psychological pressure than elegance, especially when demanding a masterpiece in exchange for silence.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The threat convinced security that a different artifact was in danger, pulling guards away from the real target.
The thief used a threat to pressure a staff member into opening a restricted door rather than risk the threatened consequences.
The letter framed the theft as an extortion plot, sending investigators after a dramatic motive instead of the real method.

trueExplanation: Missing all the painkillers and bandages, but packed with six unused cartoon-themed band-aids.
heistExplanation: Someone was meticulously prepared for every physical injury that a hurried vault escape might throw at them.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief prepared for a difficult route out, expecting cuts, falls, or a rushed climb over the outer wall.
The kit supported a risky entry through a narrow maintenance route where injury was more likely than a polite refusal.
The thief used medical supplies to create a convincing emergency, drawing a guard away from the exhibit.

item: Hidden gun in a display case
trueExplanation: It's an antique flintlock pistol that hasn't fired since 1812 and lacks any gunpowder.
heistExplanation: If a modern weapon is stashed behind a velvet display curtain, someone had rapid escalation in mind long before the alarm tripped.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief used the weapon to force a guard away from the target room without needing a prolonged fight.
A staged gunshot panic pulled guards toward the wrong display while the real theft happened elsewhere.
The weapon gave the thief enough leverage to clear an exit before the castle gates could be sealed.

item: Signs of a struggle — an overturned chair
trueExplanation: The night guard knocked it over when he jumped up after waking himself with his own snoring.
heistExplanation: A chair does not usually land upside down three meters from a desk unless someone introduced it to a sudden martial arts kick.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief knocked the guard aside in a fast struggle, gaining a brief opening to reach the protected area.
The thief staged a noisy struggle to pull security toward one office while crossing another route unseen.
The overturned chair made the first responders assume the disturbance was the crime, delaying attention to the missing artifact.

trueExplanation: The password sticker on the screen reads "Password123" – security at its absolute finest.
heistExplanation: A private collector database is basically a satellite map of human greed, complete with price tags and delivery addresses.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The database told the thief which artifact had a buyer waiting and what price the buyer would pay.
Collector delivery addresses gave the thief a ready-made destination and pickup plan after leaving the castle.
The thief used the database to create a believable false record of a private sale before the real owner noticed the loss.

trueExplanation: Made of painted glass and tin; it looks stunning under spotlights and absurd under kitchen lights.
heistExplanation: The most criminal act in a museum is sometimes not the theft itself, but replacing an original so convincingly that no one notices for weeks.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief swapped the genuine necklace for the replica, delaying discovery until a close inspection.
The substitute let the thief remove the original without leaving an empty or obviously damaged display.
Comparing the replica's flaws with the display details helped the thief identify which necklace was the real prize.

trueExplanation: The "Bypass" button is worn down to bare plastic from years of daily guard shortcuts.
heistExplanation: Everyone stares at the main alarm panel because it feels like the big boss, making it the perfect visual distraction from the side window entry.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief exploited the routinely used bypass function to pass a false all-clear through the alarm system.
A maintenance command shut down the alarm reporting function while leaving the panel looking completely normal.
The thief triggered a minor alarm fault at the panel, drawing guards there while using a side route to reach the artifact.

trueExplanation: Stamped with a student discount rate from three months ago and stuffed into a corner.
heistExplanation: A discarded ticket looks like a crucial timeline clue, but it only proves someone paid eight euros for a coffee and a quick walk.

reconstructionUses.heistExplanation: The thief used a valid visitor ticket to enter legally, then slipped from the public route into a staff-only area.
The ticket gave the thief the most convincing disguise of all: an ordinary paying visitor.
The thief used visitor timings on the ticket to move with the last group before the public galleries closed.
